title: I deleted a finished cooking menu because it broke one of my design rules
author: thezirHaze
selftext:
Solo dev on LittleBigFoot, a cozy stealth adventure. One of my five design pillars is diegetic gameplay: the fiction is the interface. Verbs are physical acts in the world, and a menu is a last resort rather than a default. He reaches into a cooler; he doesn't open a loot window.

That rule cost me a working UI. I had a cooking panel with a scrollable recipe list, ingredient counts, and Cook buttons. It functioned. I deleted it, along with its row component, because **a list of recipes where most entries show ingredients you don't have is a list of things you cannot do.** It's a menu telling you no, over and over, in a game about wandering around a park.

**What I didn't delete was the information. I moved it and changed what it withholds.**

There's still a recipe book. It just doesn't tell you how to make anything until you've made it. An undiscovered entry shows the *shape* of the answer without the identity: apple sauce reads as "TWO OF ONE INGREDIENT" until the first time you actually put two apples on a grill. Then the page fills in. A book that lists ingredients turns cooking into shopping, and you stop experimenting and start fetching.

There's also still an inventory. You can open a screen and see everything you're carrying. **The rule isn't "no menus"; it's that menus are for looking, never for doing.** When you're actually looting something, the bag is a real bag he holds open at his side, and you drag things into.

The clip is one continuous take. Reach into a cooler, take a fish and an apple. Take another apple off a grill someone else was using. Put two apples on the grate and watch them become applesauce, which nothing ever told me they would. Bag the jar.

Then take it back out and burn it on purpose, along with another apple, because **burned is a real outcome, not an error message.** Three states, raw to cooked to burned, worth nothing at the end. Cooked results obey the same rules as ingredients, so a jar of sauce can itself be ruined. And the grate's timer is world state rather than a paused session, so walking away mid-cook doesn't pause anything. Leaving is a gamble, not a menu you closed.

**The limit I had to write down next to the pillar, because taken literally it would wreck the game:** judge an interaction by the fifth time someone does it, not the first. Reaching into a cooler is great once. There are 40 hidden caches in this game, and if every one played a full reach-in animation, the rule meant to make the game feel physical would have made it a chore. Diegetic is the default, not the law. When the fiction and the fifth repetition disagree, the fifth repetition wins.

**The part that's actually about building with AI:** deleting a finished panel barely hurt, because it was cheap to produce in the first place. That's the trap. When code is fast to write, you can build the wrong thing very fast, and it will look finished. The only reason I caught this one is that the pillar was written down before the panel existed, so there was something to measure it against. Working this way makes the design document load-bearing in a way it never was when everything took a week to build.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
"**a list of recipes where most entries show ingredients you don't have is a list of things you cannot do"**

**A fair take, and one I hadn't really internalized. Though it's a fine line to walk these days in a world of internet. Minecraft for new players is not a game of discovering recipes through random application, but rather having a second monitor with the Wiki open in order to display the recipes you actually need to craft things. That being said, if the recipes are simple and intuitive enough (rather than needing specific shapes like with Minecraft) you might be able to get away with it. I hope so, because I'm also a big fan of diegetic gameplay and did an entire Skyrim VR modlist around Immersive Smithing.**

replies.author: thezirHaze
replies.body:
The wiki problem is real, but I think Minecraft proves the distinction rather than breaking it. Minecraft needs a wiki because its recipes are **arbitrary**. Nothing gets you from sticks and cobblestone to the exact 3x3 arrangement by reasoning, so of course people look it up.

Mine are guessable, which you already spotted as the escape hatch. Two apples on a grill make apple sauce. You don't need a wiki for that; you need to have once wondered what happens with two.

The hint system exists for exactly your concern: an undiscovered entry shows the **shape** without the identity. "TWO OF ONE INGREDIENT." You're not stuck, you're just not told, and the space is narrow enough that guessing beats alt-tabbing.

The thing I hold onto: you don't design against the wiki; you design so the intended path is the better experience. Designing to *defeat* lookups means deliberately obscure recipes, which is Minecraft's problem on purpose.

Respect for the Immersive Smithing list. Genuine question, since you've spent more time there than me: how did you handle repetition? Hammering a blade has to be incredible the first time and brutal by the twentieth, and that's the exact tension I had to write a limit for. VR seems like where it bites hardest.

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body: Honestly I would've gotten sick of it had it not been VR. But every game I play in VR I like having some kind of exercise element because it gives me an excuse to actually play. (Beat Saber being my most played game.) The hammering was more just a nice break between running around for quests (set up an old X box Kinect  and used a community built program that basically allowed it to detect your running in place in order to handle locomotion for open world games.) So I'd run around, kill some stuff, go to town and indulge myself in a break where I actually got to stand in place and just hammer shit for 10-20  minutes.  While I technically could've just made Smithery the majority of the game as there were economics mods and the ability to basically just play through as a shopkeep, but.. Yeh I would've gotten tired of that. The Immersive Smithing loop was  not deep enough to support doing that for longer increments IMO, as you pointed out. I think to actually inspire t hat kind of play someone would need to make a game where you're actually sculpting the blade with your hammer as you go, and etching in runework, and actually have those things matter. AI might allow for a way to actually visually judge finished products like that in the future and enable that kind of loop, but that would be quite an endeavor!
